content_voiceover: This is your summary card for hepatoblastoma, which is the most common liver tumor of childhood. The primary site is the liver itself, and the key special exam to remember is liver M R I for local staging. On risk factors, the board favorite is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, but you should also know prematurity and low birth weight, familial adenomatous polyposis caused by A P C mutation, Aicardi syndrome, constitutional trisomy eighteen, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, glycogen storage disease, Sotos syndrome, and hemihyperplasia. These are all overgrowth or growth-dysregulation syndromes, which fits the biology of a tumor arising from immature liver progenitor cells. For poor prognosis factors, remember a higher PRETEXT score, meaning more extensive pretreatment disease, multifocal primary tumor, macrovascular involvement, portal vein involvement, extrahepatic tumor extension, tumor rupture, and metastasis, a low A F P level at diagnosis which is counterintuitive but true since very low A F P can indicate a more aggressive small cell undifferentiated histology, older age at diagnosis, and histology showing small cell undifferentiated pattern, which is unfavorable, as opposed to pure fetal histology, which is the good actor. Treatment is chemotherapy plus surgery, sometimes with checkpoint inhibitors under investigation, and liver transplantation for unresectable disease confined to the liver. Overall five-year survival exceeds sixty-five percent.
keypoints: Most common liver tumor in children; liver MRI for staging
Key risk factor: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, also FAP, trisomy 18, hemihyperplasia
Poor prognosis: high PRETEXT, multifocal, vascular invasion, rupture, metastasis
Low AFP and small cell undifferentiated histology are unfavorable; pure fetal histology is favorable
keypoint_voiceover: Hepatoblastoma is the most common pediatric liver tumor, linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and other overgrowth conditions, staged with liver MRI. Poor prognosis factors include high PRETEXT score, vascular invasion, rupture, metastasis, low AFP, and small cell undifferentiated histology, while pure fetal histology is favorable. Overall five-year survival is over sixty-five percent.
